notesStmt.note: "Nat Bloom," the name that appears on the recto of the fifth leaf, was a New York City acquaintance of Whitman from as late as the 1870s, according to Edward Grier (Notebooks and Unpublished Prose Manuscripts [New York University Press, 1984] 4: 1405). If that is true, then this constitutes a very early draft of what eventually became "Old Chants," likely written in the 1860s or 70s.

Whitman never published a poem titled "America to the Old World Bards." However, another manuscript contains a draft of a poem with that title, a poem that was eventually published as "Old Chants," first appearing in the New York publication Truth on March 19, 1891. The poem was later reprinted in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891). The lines in the present manuscript have very few similarities to the published version of "Old Chants," apart from the reference to Egyptian priests and the general idea of paying homage to poets of the past. This manuscript was once part of a ten-page notebook that has since been disbound. Images of the four additional leaves of the notebook are not currently available, but are presumably blank.

lg.head: America to the Old World Bards
lg.l:
Be thy task for
once to thank, in
my name, the old
world Bards

And be thy task
to speak, to in
my name, to
preserve the
antique poems.

Let the phantoms walk through
the roads of thy soul,

Call up the ? pale ? great
procession

* Let them pas walk pass—let
the shadows walk through thy
very
soul

body.note: after the above as 1st stanzas (or canto)
the second must be a strong Invocation
Let the last stanzas of the 1st Canto be the voice of the Genius (but the identiy of that a little veiled, vague) & the words in italic

lg.l:
I hear the old
Egyptian—the priests
of in the temples
of of Memphis & Thebes

The musicians singers singing
before the Pharaos
